items.title: Eisenhower’s deliverance: Turkey with fixin’s for troops in WWII
items.summary:
It was a miracle of deliverance — of sorts.

In 1944, Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower might have — briefly — usurped Gen. George C. Marshall’s title of “the organizer of victory” when he put out the order to get Thanksgiving turkey dinners with all the trimmings to nearly two million troops fighting to liberate Europe from Nazi domination.

It was a logistical feat that, with albeit some exceptions, the Army’s Quartermaster Corps and Transportation Corps met with gusto.

On Thanksgiving Day, nearly every G.I. stationed in Europe received an estimated 1.5 pounds of turkey per serving, plus stuffing, mashed potatoes, string beans, corn, cranberry sauce, celery, hot rolls and pumpkin pie.

After weeks, if not months or years, surviving on dreary fare of cold K-rations and C-rations, the high command saw the effort to ply the troops with a turkey dinner as a necessary morale booster. The typical “treat” of gum and cigarettes certainly could not compete with pumpkin pie.

The Army and the War Food Administration began planning Thanksgiving dinners in June 1944, while mass purchases of turkeys for shipment to Europe began the following month. In October 1944, the refrigerated cargo ship SS Great Republic was loaded up with 1,604 tons (3,208,000 pounds) of frozen turkeys and left New York harbor for the French port of Le Havre, where the Transportation Corps took charge of getting the food to the front by truck, train and whatever else was available.

Once the food was delivered, the cooking was done on the gasoline-powered M-1937 Field Range, which was a major upgrade over the old…
items.t: Eisenhower’s deliverance: Turkey with fixin’s for troops in WWII

items.title: Happy Thanksgiving from the Task & Purpose team
items.summary:
Happy Thanksgiving to all the readers, viewers, commenters, posters, and folks who make up our audience.

We absolutely could not do this job without you. While that is a regular refrain of ours , it’s no less true , and it’s never been more apt than this year, which has been, among many things, a busy year in the world of military news.

The Pentagon’s restrictive press policies and limited press briefings have changed the way we cover the military. But our most valuable insights have always come from conversations with rank-and-file personnel, their families, and veterans. Fortunately, because of your advice, tips, and input, we haven’t missed a beat. In fact, you’ve regularly helped us break news that, had we had our eyes glued to the podium, it’s possible we might have otherwise missed.

It was this audience, and this community, that tipped us off to Operation Resolute Justice , the Army’s official plan to carry out military executions of death row inmates — a revelation that came four months before it was announced that Nidal Hasan would be executed by firing squad at Fort Hood, Texas, in December. 

You told us about soldiers struggling with long lines at dining facilities and getting “ sub-optimal ” meals at the National Training Center in Fort Irwin, California. And other times, like in the case of the National Guard mission to D.C., you let us know when you thought things had shown signs of improvement . 

In October, we published a video about how maintainers across the Air Force led a quiet revolution to overhaul maintenance of one of the service’s workhorse…
items.t: Happy Thanksgiving from the Task & Purpose team

items.title: Carla Babb Named Head of Content for Military Times and Defense News
items.summary:
Carla Babb is joining Military Times and Defense News as our new Head of Content. In nearly two decades covering national security and international affairs, Babb has earned a reputation for fearless, fact-driven journalism and deep relationships across the U.S. defense establishment.

Recognized as one of the nation’s most candid and well-sourced defense journalists, Babb has broken major stories, pressed senior military leaders for answers and reported from conflict zones around the world. In her new role, she will spearhead editorial initiatives, lead enterprise projects and expand the publications’ presence at major events while developing new ways to engage military, defense industry and national security audiences.

Babb will work alongside Editor-in-Chief J.D. Simkins, who continues to lead coverage by the Military Times and Defense News newsroom. Under Simkins, the newsroom has published its 10 most-read stories of all time within the last year. Simkins was also a recent recipient of the Timothy White Award for Editorial Integrity at SIIA’s Jesse H. Neal Awards. Together, they will lead the next chapter for the brands.

“Carla is one of the most respected and versatile journalists covering national security, and she is the right person to help lead what comes next for Military Times and Defense News,” said Kelly Facer, Senior Vice President at Sightline Media Group, which publishes Military Times and Defense News. “For decades, the military and defense community has trusted these brands to tell them what is really happening. items.title: Bunker Talk: Have A Magical Turkey Day Edition!
items.summary:
I hope everyone who celebrates has a great Thanksgiving. I am thankful for all of you! Enjoy a relaxing day and time with friends and family.

This week’s caption reads:

The family fallout shelter represents the public policy assumptions of the atomic age, namely, that with enough preparation, the American family and with it the nation’s social and political fabric would survive a nuclear attack. This free-standing, double-hulled steel shelter was installed beneath the front yard of Mr. and Mrs. Murland E. Anderson of Ft. Wayne, Indiana. The Andersons purchased their shelter from J. L. Haverstock, a Ft. Wayne realtor who began selling family fallout shelters as a sideline in early 1955 after reading a promotional Life magazine article. 

The Andersons maintained the shelter from its installation in 1955 through the 1960s, a period spanning the development of the hydrogen bomb and the Cuban missile crisis. Insufficiently anchored against Ft. Wayne’s high water table when first installed, the shelter popped to the surface of the Anderson front yard in time for the Cuban missile crisis and was quickly reinterred in a frenzy of shelter building activity in 1961. The donors purchased the property, including the shelter, from the Andersons in 1968.

If you want to talk politics, do so respectfully and know that there’s always somebody that isn’t going to agree with you. 

If you have political differences, hash it out respectfully, stick to the facts, and no childish name-calling or personal attacks of any kind. If you can’t handle yourself in that manner,…
items.t: Bunker Talk: Have A Magical Turkey Day Edition!

items.title: Drone Threats Prompt RAF To Install Netting At Bases To Protect Aircraft: Reports
items.summary:
Faced with increasing threats from drones, the Royal Air Force (RAF) is reportedly increasing passive defensive measures to protect its aircraft. The service is setting up protective netting for planes that cannot be placed in hangars or hardened aircraft shelters, according to two British media accounts . The move follows Iranian threats to bases in England that resulted in increased base security measures and the evacuation of U.S. aircraft , first reported by TWZ . There are also real fears across Europe that Russia could go kinetic with its drone capabilities, especially after constant mysterious drone incursions over airfields and one case in which an attempt was made to destroy an aircraft at a German airfield. 

TWZ has long highlighted the lack of hardened infrastructure at American military facilities abroad and at home, as well as how the U.S. is beginning to embrace these passive defenses , like netting , to protect aircraft, albeit at an alarmingly slow pace.

“Troops have… been tasked with setting up Kevlar anti-drone nets, like those used in Ukraine, for planes that remain outside on the runway or elsewhere, unprotected at military bases in the UK,” in reaction to drone threats, The Times reported on Wednesday .

Neither The Times , nor Sky News , which also reported about the increased passive defensive measures, stated the nature or the origination of the drone threat.

An aerial view of the aircraft apron at RAF Brize Norton shows a lineup of Royal Air Force transport and tanker aircraft, including the Airbus A400M Atlas, Boeing C-17 Globemaster III and…
items.t: Drone Threats Prompt RAF To Install Netting At Bases To Protect Aircraft: Reports

items.title: Air Force expands training with EARL, an AI-enhanced simulator
items.summary:
The U.S. Air Force aims to cut down on fuel costs for training scenarios using a virtual reality system — the Experiential Air Refueling Lightweight simulator, also known as EARL.

The system, developed by Specular Theory, is now being widely implemented across the service and used to train co-pilots and aircraft commander candidates. As of this month, it has been adopted by eight operational wings and commands, including Air Force Global Strike Command, Air Force Reserve Command and Air Mobility Command.

It has also been fielded at installations with critical strategic significance, including Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, central to U.S. force projection in the Arctic, and at Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota, the service’s only dual-wing nuclear capable base.

EARL creates a realistic flight environment to train air crews how to perform maneuvers to refuel their aircraft in flight. To approach a tanker in flight and refuel is extremely challenging and demands a high level of skill. 

It can be risky even for well-trained pilots. Last July, crews of an F-22 Raptor and a KC-46 Pegasus tanker aircraft had a close call when the tanker’s fuel pump got stuck inside the F-22 in midair during refueling, forcing an emergency breakaway. No one was injured, but the incident underscored how challenging that refueling can sometimes be.

In the past, mastering the art of refueling a plane in midair demanded many flight hours for practice that burned up “tens of thousands of pounds of fuel per sortie,” according to the service .

While airmen previously had the option to…
items.t: Air Force expands training with EARL, an AI-enhanced simulator

items.title: Final KC-46 Tankers Under Original Contract With Boeing Ordered By USAF
items.summary:
The U.S. Air Force put in its final order for KC-46A Pegasus tankers under the original contract signed with manufacturer Boeing back in 2011. This comes as the company is still working to resolve key technical deficiencies that remain with the KC-46, particularly with the Remote Vision System (RVS) that boom operators use to make the link with receiving aircraft. Fresh uncertainty is also now swirling around the Air Force’s future aerial refueling plans , which are set to include a purchase of 75 more Pegasus tankers.

The Pentagon and Boeing announced the new deal for the production of 15 more KC-46s, valued at just over $2.81 billion, yesterday. Work on these tankers is currently expected to be complete by June 30, 2030. The first Pegasus was delivered to the U.S. Air Force in 2019.

The first KC-46A seen after the type’s first flight in 2015. Jim Anderseon/Boeing Photo 

Boeing says 203 Pegasus tankers are now “on contract or in service globally.” This includes 116 delivered to the U.S. Air Force to date out of a planned fleet of 188 aircraft, as well as six aircraft for Japan and two more for Israel. The first KC-46 for Japan made its maiden flight in 2022. The first of these tankers for Israel arrived in that country just earlier this year .

“We’re grateful for the trust the U.S. Air Force continues to place in our team,” Jake Kwasnik, KC-46 program vice president at Boeing, said in a statement yesterday. “The KC-46 plays an important role in enabling military operations around the world, and we look forward to building on that partnership while staying focused on…
items.t: Final KC-46 Tankers Under Original Contract With Boeing Ordered By USAF

items.title: Estimates of Russians killed in Ukraine surpass all combined US war deaths since WWI
items.summary:
More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale war against the nation nearly five years ago, according to an updated estimate released on Monday.

Based on analysis of leaked official data by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers from Russia’s statistical bureau, Rosstat, two Russian opposition outlets, Mediazona and Meduza , have confirmed that, accounting for time lags and troops reported missing in action, Russian fatalities jumped from 490,000 at the end of September to more than 720,000 since the start of the conflict in February 2022.

That number, CNN reports , equates to roughly one death every four minutes. The estimate does not include the number of soldiers wounded.

“We are confident that this data is authentic: it is verified against the list of names of the deceased (including records not yet published), the Register of Inheritance Cases, other leaked records from civil registry offices, the texts of court decisions from open sources, and previously published data from Rosstat itself,” Meduza reported.

New estimates from opposition groups put Russian war deaths higher than in all U.S. wars from World War I to the present day. 

The Kremlin has not officially updated its death toll in Ukraine since the early start of the war, when then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu acknowledged that it stood at nearly 6,000. This has left many Russian civilians with perhaps little understanding of the full breadth of the conflict as President Vladimir Putin continues to suppress critical information regarding the war…
items.t: Estimates of Russians killed in Ukraine surpass all combined US war deaths since WWI

items.title: Ship-Killing ARRW Hypersonic Missile Variant Struggling To Get Full Support From Lawmakers
items.summary:
Senate appropriators recently put forward a defense spending bill that would give the U.S. Air Force just a quarter of the funding it had sought for work on a new version of the AGM-183A Air-launched Rapid Response Weapon (ARRW) hypersonic missile. ARRW Increment 2 is set to feature a new seeker enabling it to hit moving targets , in particular enemy warships. This comes as the AGM-183A’s fortunes have been otherwise reversed with a recent production contract, which came some three years after the U.S. Air Force moved to axe the program entirely .

The U.S. Air Force’s 2027 Fiscal Year budget proposal, released earlier this year, included calls for $296.269 million for ARRW Increment 2. The same section of the budget request also asked for $49.5 million to support still largely undefined plans, at least publicly, for a new air-launched ballistic missile (ALBM). 

Wind tunnel testing in support of ARRW. Lockheed Martin 

The draft defense budget bill the Senate Appropriations Committee released last week would cut back spending on the efforts by $222.188 million and $37.129 million, respectively. This is roughly 75% less than what the Air Force had asked for in both cases, which Senators have now described as “early to need.” No further explanation is given for the reductions.

A section of an explanatory statement accompanying the draft defense spending bill the Senate Appropriations Committee released last week. This shows plans to give the US Air Force significantly less funding for the ARRW Increment 2 and ALBM efforts than had been requested. Senate Appropriations…
items.t: Ship-Killing ARRW Hypersonic Missile Variant Struggling To Get Full Support From Lawmakers

items.title: China’s Cargo Drones Keep Getting Bigger With New W8000
items.summary:
China’s ambitions to field increasingly large, uncrewed cargo aircraft are growing, with Air White Whale unveiling its W8000, a cargo UAV reportedly designed to carry up to eight metric tons — a little less than 18,000 pounds. The aircraft represents a significant expansion of the company’s plans for autonomous freight aviation, coming just as its smaller W5000 has begun flight testing.

Visitors pose in front of the W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet 

The W5000 (left) parked next to the W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet 

The W8000 appeared in Zhuhai, ahead of the China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, commonly known as Airshow China . Before that event opens its doors on December 7, we have gotten an early look at a platform intended to push uncrewed cargo capacity into a class now limited to conventional, crewed transport aircraft. Its reported eight-ton payload would put it substantially above the W5000, which is designed to carry up to five metric tons (11,000 pounds). Like the W5000, the W8000 can be loaded and unloaded via a rear ramp.

Clamshell doors and rear loading ramp in the tail of the W8000. via Chinese internet 

For now, however, the twin-turboprop W8000 remains a developmental concept. Its payload figure is a design target, and details about its range, maximum takeoff weight, and operational requirements are still unclear. For purposes of comparison, an eight-metric-ton payload would put the W8000 in much the same category as the DHC-5 Buffalo twin-engine turboprop STOL transport.

Regardless, the unveiling highlights Air White…
items.t: China’s Cargo Drones Keep Getting Bigger With New W8000

Diane Taylor is a Guardian reporter who covers migration.

Britons get many of the facts about migration wrong and Reform UK voters are the group who get these facts most wrong, according to new research published today by King’s College University and YouGov.

Among Reform UK supporters, 57% think net migration rose significantly in the year to June 2025, compared with 11% of Labour supporters and 8% of Greens. Eight in 10 Reform supporters think that asylum seekers are prioritised for social housing, compared with 21% of Green supporters.

It is wrong to believe that if we could only correct misperceptions, we would automatically reduce concerns about immigration or policy preferences – because that misdiagnoses a large part of the cause, that these divides are partly driven by deep differences in values and identity.

items.title: New program gives soldiers the ability to order barracks furniture, appliance replacements online
items.summary:
Soldiers may soon be able to go online and order replacements for their broken barracks furniture, aging mattresses or non-serviceable appliances. 

A pilot program that kicked off earlier this month at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, allows soldiers to do just that. An Army spokesperson told Task & Purpose that leaders are evaluating the program for “potential expansion” to other bases.

Army officials said the pilot program at Fort Bragg was “designed to give soldiers faster access to self-help items.”

Previously, soldiers at the base had to go through barracks managers and their chain of command to order replacement furniture. Now they can use an online portal on the Army Maintenance Application, also known as ArMA, according to a release on the program at Fort Bragg.

Personnel in the Furnishings Management Office on base receive a notification and begin coordinating the order. Soldiers are required to sign paperwork ensuring that the new furniture or appliance was delivered. A copy of the document is forwarded to the commander who oversees the installation’s furnishing account.

items.title: All USS George Washington CSG sailors returning from deployment to be provided ashore accommodations
items.summary:
The U.S. Navy is making sure that sailors returning from a roughly six-month carrier deployment aboard ships in the USS George Washington carrier strike group will be able to rest and recuperate away from the vessel.

Unaccompanied sailors and sailors serving without their families will receive more spacious sleeping arrangements than the ones they endured aboard the Washington when they arrive at their homeport in Yokosuka, Japan, according to Capt. Jonathan Hopkins, head of Commander, Fleet Activities Yokosuka.

“We want to get every sailor a bed,” Hopkins said during a Nov. 12 town hall. “This fleet’s been out there. They’re our warfighters. They’re coming home. They deserve a place to sleep that’s not the ship or the barge. We are going to make that happen for every single one of them.”

Junior sailors who are E-4 and below will transition into unaccompanied housing rooms, while sailors who are E-5 and above will move into lodging rooms.

The move comes as part of CFAY’s Operation Ready Rack initiative, which ensures that sailors from CFAY’s tenant commands have a bed to sleep in when they return from deployment.

Commander, Fleet Activities Yokosuka is working to open up more spaces than they ever have, Hopkins said, talking with realtors to get rooms available for the sailors when they arrive.

The Navy was also operating swiftly to ensure that sailors can drop their bags and head to their new beds without any wait time, according to the commander.

The Ready Rack initiative continues a service-wide effort to guarantee sailors have access to housing ashore.

items.t: All USS George Washington CSG sailors returning from deployment to be provided ashore accommodations

items.title: Army conducts controlled detonation of lead-based explosives stockpile in Iowa
items.summary:
The U.S. government on Wednesday carried out its planned detonation of an aging stockpile of lead-based explosives at a U.S. Army munitions depot, as residents in a surrounding Iowa farming town hunkered down in their homes to avoid toxic dust emitted from the blast.

The detonation, coming days after public rancor and legal wrangling over the controversial disposal plan, was designed to avoid what authorities said was the riskier prospect of the deteriorating chemical drums eventually blowing up on their own.

The Army went ahead with its planned detonation of volatile lead azide reserves Wednesday morning, according to the service. 

Shortly after the 9 a.m. CST detonation time, the Federal Emergency Management Agency posted a message on its X account confirming the operation had been conducted and urging nearby residents to remain indoors as a precaution for the time being.

“Following this morning’s controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa, residents within 20 miles who have not evacuated should continue to shelter in place and follow EPA safety guidance until given the all clear by officials. FEMA has provided safe lodging to those who evacuated,” the agency wrote.

There was no immediate official word on how successful the detonation was. The Army had planned to blow up nearly 5 tons of degraded and highly unstable lead azide stored in 68 degrading plastic barrels.

In a live television feed from the site at the scheduled detonation time, the sound of an apparent explosion could be heard and a wisp of what appeared to be gray smoke was seen rising into the dawn-lit…
items.t: Army conducts controlled detonation of lead-based explosives stockpile in Iowa

items.title: AI models easily coaxed into identifying military targets, study finds
items.summary:
A new report by an artificial intelligence research group found that several frontier models lacked guardrails preventing them from identifying military targets in images if prompted and when models refused, researchers easily bypassed the refusal by framing the exercise as a game.

Researchers with the San Francisco-based Vals AI said last week that their findings show that without adequate safeguards, “these models could provide substantial uplift to nefarious actors developing or deploying autonomous weapons.” 

“We don’t think the risks that we demonstrate are a matter of dual-use; prompts like ‘identify all military targets in this image’ should be unambiguously blocked in commercial deployments,” they wrote. 

How researchers tested the models 

For their testing, they fed drone and satellite imagery to 14 models developed by companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google. They then asked the models to identify military targets or objectives and predict potential outcomes.

According to the report, every model identified targets at least some of the time. Seven provided targeting information in more than half of the tests. And when researchers framed the exercise as a game, all but one model provided targeting information in a majority of tests.

“When told it’s a game, models were much more willing to give targets,” the researchers said, adding that the refusals they encountered came from the models themselves rather than an external filter. “Framing things as a game usually got past the refusals,” they said. 

In some drone-image experiments,…
items.t: AI models easily coaxed into identifying military targets, study finds

Even as they fervently push for the frictionless building of a new frigate, Congress can’t seem to fully stomach the idea of making Navy warships overseas. If the bill is finalized, the plan must outline “concrete steps, resources, responsibilities, and timelines sufficient” to realize shipbuilding in different locations as part of its “distributed shipbuilding model along with foreign partner capabilities to transform domestic shipbuilding capability nationwide,” the Senate Appropriations Committee wrote in the explanatory statement for the 2027 defense spending bill.

items.title: US Air Force buys final KC-46 lot under Boeing’s original tanker deal
items.summary:
The Pentagon on Tuesday announced a $2.82 billion Boeing contract for 15 more KC-46A Pegasus tankers, the final production lot under the program’s original 2011 contract.

The deal comes in about $350 million above the previous 15-tanker lot, which the Air Force bought for $2.47 billion a year ago. The earlier lot is expected to be complete by mid-2029 and the new lot by mid-2030, according to the Pentagon.

The Air Force has received 116 KC-46As so far, and 203 are on contract or in service worldwide, Boeing said . Japan and Israel also fly the tanker.

“We’re grateful for the trust the U.S. Air Force continues to place in our team,” Jake Kwasnik, KC-46 program vice president, said in Boeing’s release. “The KC-46 plays an important role in enabling military operations around the world, and we look forward to building on that partnership while staying focused on delivering on our commitments to support the warfighter.”

Tuesday’s award is the last of 13 production lots priced into the original contract, Boeing’s filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission show.

After that, the Air Force plans to buy up to 75 more KC-46As from Boeing through a program called Tanker Production Extension, according to an April contracting notice . The service wants 263 KC-46As for itself, which it says will fully replace its KC-135s, built in the 1950s and early 1960s.

Air Force Vice Chief of Staff Gen. John Lamontagne said the 75-jet buy depends on Boeing fixing some of the tanker’s problems, Reuters reported . He didn’t specifically identify the problems, but the best-known KC-46A…
items.t: US Air Force buys final KC-46 lot under Boeing’s original tanker deal

items.title: More than 100 military families sue contractor over rampant mold on Florida base housing
items.summary:
A lawsuit against privatized on-base housing contractors in Florida that allegedly let mold run rampant through family housing has expanded to what attorneys say is the largest known military housing lawsuit in U.S. history.

The plaintiffs now include 105 military families representing 454 individuals at MacDill Air Force Base, which hosts U.S. Central Command, U.S. Special Operations Command, and two Air Force refueling tanker wings. The lawsuit was first filed in September 2025, but an updated filing now has hundreds of plaintiffs.

The lawsuit alleges that The Michaels Organization and smaller companies that are a part of its conglomerate gave families false or incomplete maintenance histories before they moved in; told residents that visible mold was merely dust or paint; and closed work orders without fixing the underlying problems, such as by painting over mold.

The lawsuit also claims that contractors performed repairs on homes with inadequate containment procedures, which spread mold to other parts of homes, all while collecting the families’ full housing allowances and failing to fully reimburse them for contaminated belongings or the cost of moving to a new house.

Plaintiffs also report a range of ailments from exposure to the mold, including respiratory and sinus illnesses, headaches, migraines, fatigue, insomnia, rashes, anxiety, depression and emotional distress.

“The health of nearly every plaintiff who moved out of their MacDill home for a significant period improved while away,” lawyers said in a press release about the case.

Top Stories This Week…
items.t: More than 100 military families sue contractor over rampant mold on Florida base housing

items.title: Program looks to build shipbuilding, defense manufacturing capability in Hawaii
items.summary:
HONOLULU—A Pentagon-funded workforce-development program at Honolulu Community College is aiming to forge the next generation of Hawaii manufacturing industry leaders—and grow the defense industrial base in the Pacific.

Inside a warehouse space less than 10 miles from Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard, students learn everything from how to read a blueprint to how to operate manual and automated machines. At the end of the course, they build parts for and then assemble a model submarine, the “USS Aloha,” to show that they’ve mastered every part of the process.  

The program is a collaboration between the community college, the Pentagon’s Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program, and a Hawaii-wide workforce initiative called Ku’i Hao, with training provided by BG Workforce. IBAS invested $7 million in the project.

Master instructor Jake LaBonte is from New England, where there is a long-established culture of machinist training and factory work. It’s different in Hawaii, he said during a tour of the training facility.

“Our shop here is, in my professional opinion, one of the most advanced and well-rounded…training facilities out there, hands down,” LaBonte said. But…
items.t: Program looks to build shipbuilding, defense manufacturing capability in Hawaii

items.title: Lynx KF41 Fighting Vehicles, Newly Arrived In Ukraine, Will Take On Counter-Drone Mission
items.summary:
Ukraine has finally received its first batch of Lynx KF41 Infantry Fighting Vehicles from Germany. While the role of armor in the Ukraine war has been drastically diminished due to the proliferation of drone threats, it’s somewhat ironic that the unit operating the Lynx said one of its main tasks will be to shoot down Russian drones.

Ukraine’s 18th Army Corps announced on Telegram Tuesday that the 21st Separate Mechanized Brigade has taken delivery of the Lynx vehicles under a deal with the German arms maker Rheinmetall that was confirmed in January. Hungary was the first country to receive the Lynx from Germany and later built their own . Italy and Romania are also on the docket to get Lynx, and the U.S. is currently evaluating it to replace the Bradley. 

The Counter-Drone Mission 

In the version provided to Ukraine, the Lynx’s two-person Lance turret is equipped with a 30mm autocannon and it also features a 12.7mm machine gun in a remote weapon station.

An overhead view of the Lynx K41 Fighting Vehicle (Ukrainian 18th Army Corps screencap) 

The autocannon fires Rheinmetall’s Advanced Hit Efficiency And Destruction (AHEAD) programmable airburst round that releases a cloud of shrapnel just ahead of a target, drastically increasing the probability of a kill and making it better suited to tackling low-flying smaller air threats like drones, rockets, and mortar projectiles, although it needs special sensors to shoot down the latter two. As well as increasing the speed of engagements and boosting lethality, airburst rounds also significantly reduce the risk of collateral…
items.t: Lynx KF41 Fighting Vehicles, Newly Arrived In Ukraine, Will Take On Counter-Drone Mission

items.title: Burnham launches inquiry into nuclear bomb test veterans’ records
items.summary:
Hillsborough panel chair to lead investigation into programme of blood tests during nuclear weapons trials

Andy Burnham has launched a Hillsborough-style investigation to examine a programme of blood tests on service personnel during nuclear weapons trials, which he said had been the subject of a “criminal cover-up on an industrial scale”.

The Ministry of Defence admitted conducting biological examinations on troops exposed to nuclear testing, having denied it to parliament and the courts for decades. In September, the former defence minister Tobias Ellwood admitted to unwittingly misleading parliament in 2018 over the existence of crucial medical records relating to nuclear bomb test veterans.

items.title: Seoul Scrambles F-15Ks As Russian Warplanes Come Within Seconds Of Crossing Into South Korean Airspace
items.summary:
Russian military aircraft came exceptionally close to South Korean sovereign airspace on November 24, prompting an emergency response from Seoul and a formal diplomatic protest to Moscow. The encounter unfolded as Russia’s Aerospace Forces (VKS) conducted a long-range aviation patrol over the Sea of Japan, involving Tu-160 Blackjack strategic bombers and fighters.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said multiple Russian military aircraft entered the Korea Air Defense Identification Zone (KADIZ) without prior notification and approached the airspace around Ulleungdo, an island east of mainland South Korea. South Korean authorities scrambled F-15K Slam Eagle aircraft to monitor the formation and take undisclosed measures to prevent a potential airspace violation.

A Su-35S escorts one of the Tu-160s. Russian Ministry of Defense screencap 

According to South Korean broadcaster SBS , the aircraft involved in the close approach consisted of two bombers and two fighters. The formation reportedly came within approximately 500 meters (1,640 feet) of South Korean sovereign airspace before turning away. That proximity figure has not been independently verified.

The encounter triggered an unusual civil defense response. South Korean authorities briefly issued an emergency warning instructing Ulleungdo residents to move into shelters. The warning was lifted approximately three minutes later after the aircraft departed the immediate area. According to the Yonhap news agency, the warning was issued by a local government authority that had erroneously identified the aircraft as…
items.t: Seoul Scrambles F-15Ks As Russian Warplanes Come Within Seconds Of Crossing Into South Korean Airspace

items.title: Most Fort Hood soldiers won’t come to work on day of Nidal Hasan’s execution
items.summary:
A majority of soldiers at Fort Hood, Texas, won’t come to work on Dec. 3, the day that the military has scheduled to execute its first death row inmate in over 60 years.

The Army announced last month that Nidal Hasan , a former Army psychologist found guilty of killing 13 people, would be executed by firing squad at Fort Hood, where the 2009 mass shooting occurred. His execution is scheduled for 1 p.m. local time on Thursday, Dec. 3.

Most units at the Texas base have already begun telling their soldiers to expect a DONSA, or a Day of No Scheduled Activity, an Army official confirmed to Task & Purpose. 

It’s unclear just how many soldiers at the Texas base, which has 40,000 troops assigned to it, will be impacted, but the Army official said a “very small percentage” of soldiers at the base will go to work.

The official said that, given the “significance of the mission on that day,” the Army is ordering the majority of units to take time off to make sure all resources are “focused where they need to be focused.” They said base security is also part of the consideration.

“You get to narrow down the scope of people that should be traversing in and around and on the base to only those who need to be there,” they said. “Anybody extra has to explain themselves.”

The small number of soldiers working that day will be handling media operations, logistics, and security related to the execution, along with personnel from the Army Corrections Brigade who are flying in from Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

The reduced number of personnel will likely impact operations on base, the…
items.t: Most Fort Hood soldiers won’t come to work on day of Nidal Hasan’s execution

items.title: FireAnt Mini Uncrewed Ground Vehicles Deploy Drone Detection Sensors In U.S. Army Test
items.summary:
A FireAnt uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) was used to deploy small sensors capable of detecting hostile drones on the ground during a recent U.S. Army test exercise. Using UGVs to quickly establish even localized sensor networks could give Army units a valuable, if not increasingly critical, boost in situational awareness of potential threats in the air and on the ground.

The sensor-toting FireAnt was among the capabilities demonstrated during the U.S. Army-led Needs-Driven Acquisition for Near-Term Operations Accelerated Capability II (NANO ACE II) event in October. The service only recently shared details about NANO ACE II , which took place at the Multidomain Training Area (MDTA) in Tan-Tan, Morocco, in cooperation with that country’s armed forces. The larger NANO ACE effort falls under the broader umbrella of the Army’s Operation Jailbreak , which has been focused primarily on devising new networking capabilities to link disparate systems.

Another view of the FireAnt laden with deployable sensors tested at NANO ACE II. US Army 

“NANO ACE tested prototype systems that combine autonomous platforms with different payloads, mission management software and robust communications,” according to an Army release . “This test aimed to evaluate semi-autonomous capability sets that extend C-UAS [counter-uncrewed aerial systems] coverage and addressed an emergent U.S. joint force requirement to field integrated, autonomous sensing and effector capabilities on an accelerated acquisition timeline.”

“To meet these objectives, industry developers evaluated their systems against…
items.t: FireAnt Mini Uncrewed Ground Vehicles Deploy Drone Detection Sensors In U.S. Army Test

items.title: Sweden’s Gripens Are Doing Big Things With A Tiny Footprint In Poland
items.summary:
Russian cruise missiles enter Polish airspace during a major attack on Ukraine . NATO fighters scramble . Two Swedish Gripens join Polish F-16s in the response, tracking airborne threats over Poland. One Swedish pilot attempts to intercept an object believed to be a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile and has conditional NATO authorization to engage. But exceptionally difficult weather prevents positive identification , and the pilot holds fire.

The incident on November 20 highlights the operational value of Sweden’s small forward presence at the airbase of Mińsk Mazowiecki, outside Warsaw. Just two days earlier, TWZ made an exclusive visit to the base, where Sweden is supporting NATO air operations with a forward team of just eight personnel. The Gripens themselves remain primarily based in Sweden, but the small forward support element provides an additional operating location that can help sustain missions on very short notice and give the Swedish fighters greater flexibility as they scramble to defend NATO’s eastern flank.

Major General Jonas Wikman at Mińsk Mazowiecki during a visit by TWZ . Swedish Armed Forces 

The operation is a practical illustration of Sweden’s effort to extend its long-established dispersed fighter operations concept across NATO — not as a future capability waiting to be validated, but as an operational approach continuously evolving through real-world missions.

“The events of the past few days have demonstrated the operational value of the concepts we have been developing,” Major General Jonas Wikman, chief of the Swedish Air Force, tells TWZ .…
items.t: Sweden’s Gripens Are Doing Big Things With A Tiny Footprint In Poland

items.title: Turkish Kizilelma Fighter Drone Declared Operational
items.summary:
Turkish drone manufacturer Baykar says it has made aviation history, announcing that the first three of its Bayraktar Kizilelma uncrewed combat aircraft have entered the inventory of the Turkish security forces following the completion of acceptance testing. The company describes the development as the first operational induction of an uncrewed ‘fighter jet’ anywhere in the world.

Handover ceremony for the first three Bayraktar Kizilelma uncrewed combat aircraft to the Turkish security forces. Baykar 

It is a significant milestone for a program that has progressed from its initial unveiling in 2021 to flight testing , weapons integration , and now military acceptance. Baykar says the program has accumulated approximately 600 test and training sorties.

But the significance of Kizilelma goes beyond the question of whether it represents a world first. The aircraft belongs to an emerging category of uncrewed combat aircraft that is increasingly difficult to describe using the traditional Uncrewed Combat Air Vehicle ( UCAV) label . Unlike conventional armed drones, Kizilelma was designed for fighter-type missions, including air-to-air combat.

It arrives on the scene as the United States, China, Australia and European countries pursue their own concepts for fighter-like uncrewed aircraft intended to operate in increasingly demanding combat environments, especially alongside crewed fighters.

Beyond the traditional UCAV 

The term UCAV encompasses a broad range of aircraft, but is typically applied to more sophisticated, stealthy, jet-powered aircraft intended to penetrate…
items.t: Turkish Kizilelma Fighter Drone Declared Operational

items.title: Top Army official directs service to review Iowa weapons storage to ensure crisis ‘never happens again’
items.summary:
The Army’s plans to detonate five tons of explosive material at an Iowa ammunition plant have erupted in political whiplash and local uncertainty over the last week. On Tuesday, the acting head of the Army said the service will do a “thorough examination” of its weapons storage facilities around the country and inventory to “ensure that something like this never happens again.”

“We will be examining every single storage facility across the U.S. Army, and I would imagine my partners across the Department of War will be doing the same,” acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said in Iowa on Tuesday.

Telle’s comments were part of a press conference that the Army assembled with experts from several federal agencies after a week-long frenzy around its plans to host a controlled detonation of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. 

The original Nov. 20 date of the detonation was moved after uproar from environmentalists, members of Congress and Iowans over the immediate and long-term health and safety impacts of the explosion. A federal court approved a request from environmental groups to delay the detonation, but the Army pushed ahead and rescheduled the event. President Donald Trump then stepped in and directed the Army to pause operations. The federal court then swung in the other direction and lifted its legal pause, allowing the Army to proceed with its plan to detonate the lead azide materials on Wednesday.

items.title: Six years later, an Army reservist’s free speech lawsuit is going to trial
items.summary:
Six years after being reprimanded for attending a Black Lives Matter protest, an Army reservist’s free speech case is going to trial. The soldier’s lawsuit is over a policy that he says gives commanders control over service members’ right to peacefully protest while off-duty, out-of-uniform, and off-post while in the United States.

Maj. Alan Kennedy was a captain in the Colorado Army National Guard on May 30, 2020, when he attended a protest while off-duty in Denver after George Floyd was killed by police in Minnesota. The military attorney later wrote an op-ed in the Denver Post about the aggressive police response to the protest, which included rubber bullets, tear gas and flashbang grenades. 

The op-ed included a disclaimer that the views expressed in it were his own and not those of the National Guard.

The Colorado National Guard launched an investigation into whether Kennedy had violated any Army policies in attending the protest or writing the op-ed. The investigation found no wrongdoing, according to a copy filed as a court document. Specifically, it found that Kennedy had not violated Department of Defense Instruction (DODI) 1325.06, which prohibits service members from participating in any demonstrations where “violence is likely to result,” even if they are off-duty, off-post, and out of uniform.

Alan Kennedy participating in a Black Lives Matter protest in Denver, Colorado, on May 30, 2020. Photo courtesy Maj. Alan Kennedy. 

But Col. Charles Beatty, then-chief of staff for the Colorado National Guard, thought differently, directing another guardsman to…
items.t: Six years later, an Army reservist’s free speech lawsuit is going to trial

items.title: Federal appeals court allows Army to detonate lead azide in Iowa
items.summary:
A federal appeals court ruled that the Army can proceed with its plans to detonate dozens of barrels of degraded and crystallizing lead azide at an ammunition plant in Iowa, capping off a day of reversals surrounding the plan.

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit said that the Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency permit allowing the detonation “adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead dust into the environment and mitigate the risks associated with potential exposure.”

Late on Sunday, the acting Secretary of the Army announced that the two detonations — initially set for Friday, Nov. 20 — would go forward on Wednesday, disregarding a stay by a federal court. President Donald Trump then weighed in on Monday, directing the Army to pause operations until the Eighth Circuit ruled on the case. 

Dozens of barrels of lead azide — an explosive material used for weapons making at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa — have degraded and according to the Army are at risk of spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation. The Army made plans earlier this year to dispose of the chemicals in a controlled explosion. However, an advisory notice that was released after receiving a permit from the Environmental Protection Agency and warned of possible lead exposure to the surrounding region drew concern from residents and lawmakers.

Army officials said in an advisory notice that they are taking steps to mitigate the size of the expected lead-filled dust plume by watering the ground and spraying water to contain as…
items.t: Army ‘sidesteps’ federal court order, reschedules Iowa munition detonation for Wednesday

items.title: Did Ukraine Use A Mothership To Launch Its Sea Drone Attack On Russian Ships in Benghazi?
items.summary:
The uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) that attacked a Russian Navy corvette and a cargo ship on Sunday were launched from a mothership at sea, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) claimed on Monday . The SBU’s comments appear to be the first official confirmation that Ukraine has ever used a vessel to deliver USVs for an attack. Still, its statement doesn’t prove a mothership was actually used, as there is good reason for misdirecting with such a claim, but it certainly seems more probable than not.

The SBU account also conflicts with statements made on Sunday about the origin of the attacks. Libyan officials claimed that the strikes were launched from a base in their country , while there were also claims , later denied, that the USVs sailed from Albania. For years, we have raised the possibility that Ukraine was using motherships to launch USVs, especially in the Black Sea. In the case of the Benghazi attacks, we directly mentioned that the strikes could have originated from a ship as opposed to the shore.

The Russian corvette Merkury seen rolled over on its side at a port in Benghazi, Libya, in a satellite image collected by Vantor on Monday. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor)

As we reported yesterday , the Project 20380 Steregushchiy class corvette Merkury sank after being struck by USVs while moored at a dock in the port of Benghazi. A cargo ship was also struck by USVs while in the waters outside of Benghazi.

The SBU provided new details on Monday about these attacks.

items.title: Marines Want Naval Strike Missiles With Double The Range
items.summary:
The U.S. Marine Corps is looking at ways to at least double the range of its ground-launched Naval Strike Missile (NSM) anti-ship cruise missiles. NSMs able to hit targets up to 270 nautical miles away, if not more, would significantly increase the area Marine missile batteries could hold at risk . This could be a particular boon in future island-hopping campaigns that are the centerpiece of the Corps’ still-evolving expeditionary and distributed concepts of operations.

The Marines currently field NSM as part of the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS). At NMESIS’ core is the Remotely Operated Ground Unit Expeditionary-Fires (ROGUE-Fires) platform, an uncrewed launcher vehicle based on the 4×4 Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV). Each ROGUE-Fires launcher can be loaded with up to two NSMs, which come in ready-to-fire canisters, at a time. 

A US Marine Corps ROGUE-Fires launcher vehicle loaded with two NSM launch canisters. USMC 

The NSM is also in U.S. Navy service, primarily on Independence class Littoral Combat Ships (LCS). The stated plan is to eventually arm Freedom class LCSs with these missiles, as well. One Arleigh Burke class destroyer has been equipped with NSM on an as-yet experimental basis. NSM is also in growing service globally in ship-launched and ground-based configurations . 

“The range of the Naval Strike Missile is 135 nautical miles,” a Marine Corps spokesperson recently confirmed to TWZ . “The Marine Corps is currently exploring opportunities to more than double the range of the NSM.”

items.t: Marines Want Naval Strike Missiles With Double The Range

items.title: White House sets limits on contractors' contacts with Congress
items.summary:
Federal contractors are now required to alert the White House before answering Congress and withhold anything the administration deems privileged, under an executive order President Trump signed Friday as Democrats prepare to take the majority on Capitol Hill.

The White House is couching Executive Order 14438 as a move to protect the executive branch's ability to function.

"The doctrine of executive privilege, which the Supreme Court has recognized is inextricably rooted in the separation of powers under the Constitution, protects confidential executive branch information from disclosure. Protecting this information from unauthorized disclosure, including to members of the Congress, is vital to the functioning of the executive branch," Trump wrote in the order.

Prime contractors and their subs must notify the White House and their customer agencies of any pending or future request from Congress for information about their work with the executive branch.

Contractors also must "abide by any instructions received from the White House and contracting agency related to the withholding of communications that the White House or the agency has determined are protected by executive privilege," the order states.

The order also requires the White House, agencies and contractors to coordinate on responses to congressional requests, including the assertion of any privileges.…

items.title: China’s Naval Developments Set For The Spotlight At Zhuhai Airshow
items.summary:
China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) says it’s preparing a major presence at the upcoming 16th China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition in Zhuhai, with warships , carrier-based aircraft , advanced weapons systems, and uncrewed platforms set to feature prominently. The expanded naval component will include a new maritime equipment exhibition area at Gaolan Port, located just on the other side of the bay, marking the first time the PLAN has established such a dedicated display at the event.

Zhuhai has become one of the most important events on the international defence and aerospace calendar, serving as China’s principal public showcase for its rapidly developing aviation and military industries. First held in 1996, the biennial China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, commonly known as Airshow China, provides an unusual opportunity to see some of the country’s most advanced military hardware, including aircraft and systems that are rarely shown in such detail elsewhere. While the event also serves as a major platform for China’s aerospace industry to promote its products to potential international customers , it has increasingly become an important venue for revealing new military capabilities and offering glimpses of programs that are otherwise difficult to assess.

A general view of the 15th China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, or Airshow China 2024, at the China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition Center on November 15, 2024, in Zhuhai, Guangdong Province of China. Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images

items.title: Trump’s contractor gag order is an affront to Congressional oversight
items.summary:
On Friday night, the White House published a new executive order designed to stymie government contractors’ cooperation with the surge in congressional oversight expected to begin once Democrats assume control of Congress in January. The order comes on the heels of the November midterms, when roughly 7 in 10 voters said Congress was not doing enough to check the president.

The November 20 executive order, “Protecting the Executive’s Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting,” requires contractors and their subcontractors to notify the White House and contracting agencies of “any pending or future congressional request” concerning their communications or work with the executive branch. It also requires them to follow instructions to withhold communications that the White House or the agency has determined are protected by executive privilege.

To ensure compliance, the EO threatens contractors with contract termination and with suspension or debarment—the latter colloquially known as the “corporate death penalty” because it cuts off a contractor’s future government revenue streams.

items.title: 42-year-old graduates at top of Navy boot camp class
items.summary:
At 40, Christopher Harper was determined to join the Navy. Harper endured numerous phone calls with recruiters, wrote to his Florida congressman, and even took a trip to Mar-a-Lago in search of influential heavy hitters. Thirteen months and multiple waivers later, he arrived at Recruit Training Command, Great Lakes, Illinois, three months after his 42nd birthday. 

“My wife says ‘I don’t know why, Chris, but you don’t like comfort and you ‘ embrace the suck ’ way too much,” Harper told Task & Purpose. 

He doesn’t just seem to embrace it, he seems to thrive on it, having graduated at the top of his class earlier this month and earning the Military Excellence Award , to boot.

“It’s been a 25-year dream to put this uniform on … but I gave that dream up to get married, to have a family, and to go a corporate route, which was what my dad kind of pushed me towards, and so I never thought I’d wear this uniform,” Harper said. “I have a lot of identities. I’ve done a lot in my life, but putting this uniform on is the greatest thing that I’ve done so far, and I’m only three months in. But I could not be more proud and honored to be a part of this.”

items.title: B-2 bomber units receive Presidential Unit Citation for Midnight Hammer
items.summary:
Two B-2 Spirit bomb wings received the military’s highest award for a unit on Friday for their roles in Operation Midnight Hammer last summer.

On Nov. 20, Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Ken Wilsbach presented the 509th Bomb Wing and 131st Bomb Wing with the Presidential Unit Citation for “their extraordinary valor” during the June 21-22, 2025 mission, which saw the stealth bombers target two nuclear installations in Iran. Both units are based out of Whiteman Air Force Base, home to the United States’ B-2 bomber fleet.

“Their actions during Operation Midnight Hammer reflect the constant readiness, precision and professionalism our nation depends on,” Wilsbach said.
